932.title: Harvest home
932.hook: harvest festivals and Thanksgiving mark the end of the year's work
932.howItsDone: At harvest festivals, churches and communities decorate with produce, sing harvest hymns and share a meal, and the gifts are sometimes given away; Thanksgiving brings families together around a shared table.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukkot: a roof of branches, more shade than sun, and room for the stranger. Your line was the booth. Have you found your meal outside yet? Today, the moment the last load comes in. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

Harvest home. In English country tradition, those two words named a moment: the last wagon of sheaves coming up the lane toward the barn, and the field finally bare. Tradition says a supper followed, for everyone who had worked the field, the farmer and the laborers at one table. The words made their way into hymns. In the United States and Canada, a Thanksgiving table can still carry some of that feeling: a season's work done, and a meal to mark it. Today: harvest home.
screen: `THE LAST LOAD COMES IN.` → `ONE TABLE FOR EVERYONE.` → `HARVEST HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the song. An English hymn by Henry Alford puts today's word in its second line: "Come, ye thankful people, come, Raise the song of harvest home: All is safely gathered in, Ere the winter storms begin." Notice what it celebrates. Not the profit. The relief. The work is done, and done in time. Second, the tears behind it. A psalm puts the harvest in a longer story. In the King James words: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." The sowing was hard. Some of it happened in bad years and worried seasons. The joy at harvest is the same field, seen from the other end. Third, the full table. Deuteronomy pictures a people settled in a good land and eating their fill, and says, in the King James words: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." The next verses warn why: a full house is where forgetting starts. So the thanks is set at the moment of plenty, not only in the lean years. Jewish tradition takes this verse as the root of the blessing said after meals. Fourth, your own field. You may never bring in wheat. But a year of work has a harvest too: a project finished, a child grown a little, a skill that wasn't there before, a hard season gotten through. And some of it may have been sown in tears. A harvest festival is a pause to look at what's gathered, call it by name, and give thanks, before the next season starts.
screen: `ALL IS SAFELY GATHERED IN.` · `SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.` · `BLESS WHEN YOU ARE FULL.` · `YOUR OWN FIELD.` · then, large: `HARVEST HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Look back over this year of your work, paid or unpaid. Let three things you've gathered come to mind, one at a time. Something finished. Something learned. Something survived. Name each one, quietly. If one of them was sown in tears, let that be part of it. Then think of one person who helped you bring it in, and let their face come to mind. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words. If not, just say thank you, to whoever comes to mind. The bell holds the time.
Harvest home. The old name for the moment the last load is in, with a supper and thanks for the year's work. Today's word.
Your line: harvest home. Today, tell one person something you gathered this year, and thank someone who helped you bring it in. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: Pongal, the harvest
933.hook: a Tamil harvest festival thanking the sun and the cattle; the rice pot boils over for luck
933.howItsDone: At Pongal, Tamil families draw kolam patterns at the door, cook new rice with milk and jaggery in a new pot facing the sun until it boils over, call out "Pongalo Pongal", and honor their cattle on a day of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, harvest home: the last load in, a supper, and a blessing at the full table. Your line was harvest home. What did you name from your year? Today, a harvest in South India, and a pot that's meant to spill. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

Early morning in a courtyard in Tamil Nadu. A pattern of rice flour, a kolam, has been drawn on the ground outside the door. A new clay pot sits over a fire, facing the rising sun, with turmeric leaves tied around its neck. Inside: new rice, milk, and jaggery. The whole family is watching it. Nobody is stirring. They're waiting for the moment it rises to the rim and spills over the side. When it does, they shout. Today: Pongal.
screen: `A KOLAM AT THE DOOR.` → `A NEW POT FACING THE SUN.` → `EVERYONE WATCHING IT SPILL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Pongal is both the festival and the sweet rice dish cooked for it. Tamils keep it as the month of Thai begins, when the harvest is in, and it runs over several days. Second, the sun. The main day thanks the sun, Surya, for the harvest. The pot is set out in the open, facing east. The first rice of the new crop is cooked and offered before it's eaten. The meal begins with thanks to the light the fields depend on. Third, the cattle. A day is set aside for the cows and bullocks that pulled the plows. They're washed, their horns are painted, they're hung with bells and flowers, and they're fed some of the sweet rice. The animals who did the work get thanked like workers, because they were. Fourth, the overflow. Tradition says the pot boiling over is a good sign, a picture of a household where good things spill beyond the rim. People call out Pongalo Pongal as it rises. Usually, a pot boiling over is a mess to clean up. Here, it's the whole point. The Tamil classic, the Thirukkural, has a chapter in praise of farming. In paraphrase, one of its couplets says that however far the world wanders, it still follows the plow. Pongal is the day the world turns around and thanks the plow, the sun and the ox, and lets the pot run over.
screen: `THE FESTIVAL AND THE DISH.` · `THANKS TO THE SUN.` · `THANKS TO THE CATTLE.` · `LET IT SPILL.` · then, large: `PONGALO PONGAL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Picture the pot on the fire, the milk rising slowly, the family waiting. Now think of one good thing in your life that has been sitting just under the rim. A thank-you you haven't said. A compliment you've kept to yourself. Some time, or money, or food you could share. Let it rise in your mind. Then decide where it could spill over today, and to whom. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for whatever feeds you. The bell holds the time.
Pongal. The Tamil harvest festival and its sweet rice, cooked until it boils over, with thanks to the sun and the cattle. Today's word.
Your line: boil over. Today, let one good thing spill past the rim: say the thanks, give the compliment, share the food. Don't stir it down. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: Your work, written
934.hook: what is your work, really, beyond the job title?
934.howItsDone: People who write down their real work usually keep it to one plain sentence about what they do for others, put it somewhere visible, and revisit it when their work or stage of life changes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pongal: a pot of new rice left to spill, and thanks to the sun and the cattle. Your line was boil over. What did you let spill? Today, the work block starts to close, with one question. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

So, what do you do? It's the first question at a party, and the easy answer is a job title. Accountant. Nurse. Student. Between jobs. Retired. The title is true, but it's thin. It doesn't say that the accountant is the one who stays calm when a family's finances fall apart, or that the student is quietly holding a household together. For weeks now, this path has looked at work through scripture, craft, festivals and harvest. Before the block closes, one question is left: what is your work, really? Today: your work.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `THE TITLE IS THIN.` → `WHAT IS YOUR WORK, REALLY?`

segments.voice: First, an essayist on calling. Ralph Waldo Emerson, in his essay Spiritual Laws, puts it in two short sentences: "Each man has his own vocation. The talent is the call." A vocation, in his sense, isn't a title someone hands you. It's what you're fitted for, the one direction, he says, in which all space opens. A title can match it, or only sit somewhere near it. Second, a job description in one line. The prophet Micah sums up what God asks in a single sentence. In the King James words: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Three verbs. No job title at all. And yet it could sit on top of all sorts of jobs. Third, the gap. Between the title and the real work, there's usually a gap. A teacher's title is teacher; her work might be making sure no child feels stupid. A bus driver's title is driver; his work might be getting tired people home safely, and being a kind face at the end of a long day. The title is what's on the badge. The real work is what you'd want someone to say you did. Fourth, writing it down. One line is enough. Short enough to remember, plain enough to check against a Tuesday. It isn't a mission statement for a boss. It's a sentence for you, and it can change as your stage of life changes. Emerson's was for anyone with a talent. Micah's was for a whole people. Yours only has to be true.
screen: `THE TALENT IS THE CALL.` · `DO JUSTLY, LOVE MERCY, WALK HUMBLY.` · `THE BADGE AND THE REAL WORK.` · `ONE LINE IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `YOUR WORK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Say your job title to yourself, or whatever you'd answer at a party. Then set it aside. Ask: when my work is going well, what am I really doing for people? Let a few answers come and go. Keeping things safe. Making things clear. Helping someone heal, or learn, or rest. Look for the one that's truest. Shape it into one plain line. When the bell rings, write that line down, on paper or in your phone. The bell holds the time.
Your work. Not the title on the badge, but what you're really doing for people, written in one line. Today's word.
Your line: my real work. Keep the sentence you wrote somewhere you'll see it, and check one task today against it. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

935.title: Service at work
935.howItsDone: Some Christians serve at food banks, hospitals and prisons with Matthew 25 in mind; in Islam, small acts of help count as sadaqa, charity; others look for service by naming who their everyday work helps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your work: Emerson's talent as a call, Micah's three verbs, and one line beneath the job title. Your line was my real work. Did you write yours down? Today, a question that line points to: who is it for? Day nine hundred thirty-five.

Who is a spreadsheet for, at eleven at night? Or a line of code nobody will ever read, a pallet of boxes in a warehouse, a form stamped and filed? Some work seems far from any human face. Yet follow it far enough and there's usually someone at the other end. The spreadsheet decides whether a family's loan goes through. The code keeps a hospital's records from crashing. The boxes are somebody's birthday present. A job serves someone, even when the someone is out of sight. Today: service at work.
screen: `A SPREADSHEET AT ELEVEN.` → `FOLLOW IT FAR ENOUGH.` → `SOMEONE AT THE OTHER END.`

segments.voice: First, a surprise at the end of a story. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells of a king who welcomes people for what they did: they fed the hungry, gave the thirsty a drink, took in a stranger, visited the sick and the prisoner. They're puzzled. In the King James words: "Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?" The king answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Christians read the least of these in more than one way. What the story itself stresses is the surprise: they served without knowing who was at the other end. Second, a hand with the luggage. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari lists small acts that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, counted as charity. In paraphrase: helping someone onto his animal, or lifting his bags up to him, is charity. A good word is charity. Moving something harmful out of the road is charity. None of it needs a title. Just a person nearby who needs a hand. Third, the hidden line. Your work may not look like feeding the hungry. But the same thread runs through a desk job: somewhere down the line, a person is helped, or not, by how you do it. Naming that person changes the task. Fourth, the difference it makes. A form filed for nobody is a chore. The same form filed so a widow gets her pension on time is service. The job hasn't changed. What changes is that you can see who's at the other end. In Matthew's story, the helpers never saw who it was. Today's practice tries to.
screen: `THE LEAST OF THESE.` · `LIFTING SOMEONE'S BAGS IS CHARITY.` · `SOMEONE AT THE END OF THE LINE.` · `NAME THEM, AND THE TASK CHANGES.` · then, large: `SERVICE AT WORK.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Pick one ordinary task you'll do today, paid or unpaid, maybe one you'd rather skip. Now picture one person it's for, sitting right in front of you, the way you'd set a plate down in front of a guest. Not a crowd. One person, close enough to hand it to. Notice whether the task looks any different with them sitting there. Stay with them for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words. If not, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Service at work. A job serves someone; naming who turns a task into service. Today's word.
Your line: who it serves. Before one task today, name the person at the other end, out loud or on paper. Then do it for them. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: Work as practice
936.hook: a task done with attention is practice
936.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries, monks and visitors do samu, a period of cleaning, gardening and kitchen work done in silence as meditation; Christians drawn to Brother Lawrence try to keep God in mind through ordinary tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, service at work: the least of these, and a hand with someone's bags. Your line was who it serves. Whose face did you find at the end of a task? Today, what happens inside you while you do it. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

Before he ever cooked for monks, he was a footman, and by his own account a great clumsy fellow who broke everything. Later, as a lay brother in a Paris monastery, he was sent to the kitchen, work he says he naturally disliked. A few weeks ago, at the start of this block, we met him there, in the clatter. Brother Lawrence. Today, something smaller he said: about an egg in a pan, and about what to do when the mind wanders off. Today: work as practice.
screen: `A CLUMSY FOOTMAN.` → `SENT TO THE KITCHEN.` → `AN EGG IN A PAN.`

segments.voice: First, the omelet. Brother Lawrence's letters and conversations were gathered into a small book, The Practice of the Presence of God. In paraphrase, he says we needn't do great things: he turns his little omelet in the pan for the love of God. The size of the task isn't the point. And when he notices he has wandered, he doesn't scold himself or make a show of being sorry. He simply comes back. Second, the monastery work period. In Zen monasteries in Japan, there's a name for the hours spent sweeping, weeding, cleaning and cooking: samu, work practice. It isn't a break from meditation. It is meditation, with a broom. The same attention given to the breath on a cushion is given to the corner of the floor. Third, the dishes. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh wrote about washing dishes. In paraphrase, his point was this: there are two ways to wash the dishes. One is to wash them to get them clean, so you can get on to the next thing. The other is to wash the dishes to wash the dishes, fully there for the warm water and the plate in your hand. Only the second, he said, is really being alive while you do it. Fourth, what makes a task practice. Not the task. A Christian cook, a Zen monastery and a Vietnamese teacher each speak from their own tradition, and each points at attention. Any task, done with full attention and coming back when you drift, can become practice. Over these weeks we've looked at why we work, and who for. This is about how.
screen: `A LITTLE OMELET, FOR THE LOVE OF GOD.` · `SAMU: MEDITATION WITH A BROOM.` · `WASH THE DISHES TO WASH THE DISHES.` · `PRACTICE IS ATTENTION.` · then, large: `WORK AS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. For now, the breath is the task. Follow it in and out, the way Brother Lawrence turned the omelet: just this one, now. When the mind drifts to something else, notice where it went, and come back, without scolding. Then come back again. The coming back is the whole exercise. Near the end, choose one small task for later today, dishes, a report, sweeping, an email, to do this same way. The bell holds the time.
Work as practice. A task done with full attention, coming back each time you drift, becomes a practice. Today's word.
Your line: work as practice. Do the one task you picked as practice today, start to finish, and each time your mind drifts, come back to your hands. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Different answers
937.hook: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood: the traditions see work differently
937.howItsDone: People on different paths describe their work through their own tradition's lens: some as a calling, some as an offering or a duty, some as an honest livelihood, and some as simply hard and necessary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, work as practice: one ordinary task, done with your whole attention. Your line was work as practice. Which task did you pick? Today, every answer we've heard about work, laid on one table. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

A lunch break, and five coworkers share a bench outside the building. Ask each of them what their work really is, underneath the job title. The first says: it's the price of being alive. The second: it's what I was made for. The third: I do it for someone else, not for me. The fourth: it's my part, and somebody has to do it. The fifth shrugs: it pays the rent, and I try to earn it honestly. Nobody in that line is wrong. Over these weeks on work, each of those five answers has turned up in a tradition we've visited. Today, before we close the question, all five go side by side.
screen: `FIVE PEOPLE, ONE BENCH.` → `FIVE ANSWERS.` → `ALL FIVE, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the curse. In Genesis, outside the garden, the ground turns hard, and the King James words are blunt: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." Some readers hear a punishment there. Others hear plain honesty: work is hard. Second, the calling. Martin Luther taught that a milkmaid or a cobbler serving the neighbor is doing holy work, and the letter to the Colossians puts it like this: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Third, the offering. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever he does, whatever he eats or gives, can be done as an offering. The work goes up like a gift, and the result stops being the point. Fourth, the duty. The Gita again: better your own duty done imperfectly than someone else's done well. Your work is your part, and the part matters more than the applause. Fifth, livelihood. The Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons. Earn a living, in a way that doesn't harm. Now the part worth noticing. These aren't five rival theories where one has to win. The Gita itself holds two of them, offering and duty, in the same book. A nurse can call her work a calling and still feel the sweat of it at the end of a night shift. And the answer can change with the season of a life, or the day of the week. On a Monday it's sweat. On a good Thursday, it might be an offering.
screen: `THE SWEAT OF THY FACE.` · `DO IT HEARTILY.` · `AS AN OFFERING, AS A DUTY.` · `EARN IT WITHOUT HARM.` · then, large: `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Wherever you are, let your breathing slow. Hear the five words again, one at a time: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood. Don't choose yet. Let your own work pass by each word, the way you'd hold a shirt up in front of a mirror. Which one fits today? Maybe it's sweat. Maybe it's a calling you'd forgotten about. Maybe it's two of them. When one settles, keep it, and let the others rest for now. If you pray, you can offer that word in your own tradition's way. The bell holds the time.
Different answers. Curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood: the traditions see work in different ways, and a person can hold more than one. Today's word.
Your line: different answers. Today, when work gets heavy, notice which answer you reach for, and try one of the others for an hour. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

938.title: Work close
938.hook: sixty days on work, and the last move: finish, look, rest
938.howItsDone: Several traditions pair work with set times of rest: the Jewish Sabbath, Christian Sunday rest, Friday congregational prayer in Islam, monastic hours of prayer, and Buddhist observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, five answers side by side: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood. Your line was different answers. Which one fit your work this week? Today, we close the question. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

A carpenter sets down the plane, runs a palm along the tabletop, and steps back. Not to start the next job. Just to look. That small pause, between the last stroke and the next thing, is where this whole stretch on work ends. When this stretch began, we met a garden that needed tending. Since then: a craftsman filled with spirit, a tentmaker, a farmer Guru, a woodworker who fasted before he carved, a Chan master who wouldn't eat on a day he didn't work. This week alone, a harvest, a written answer to what your work really is, service, attention, and five different answers. Today, the last move. Finish. Look. Rest.
screen: `STEP BACK AND LOOK.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON WORK.` → `FINISH. LOOK. REST.`

segments.voice: First, finishing. Back on day eight hundred eighty-six, Rabbi Tarfon said it isn't yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop. That's true of the big work: justice, a family, a life. But inside the big work are small things that can be finished. A drawer. A letter. A report. Finishing one is its own kind of practice. Second, looking. Again and again in the creation story, Genesis pauses to look. And at the end of the sixth day, the King James says: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." The work isn't over until someone looks at it. Not to find the flaw. To see it. Third, rest. The next verses don't start a new project. "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made." In that story, rest isn't what's left when the work runs out. It's part of the shape. Fourth, the whole block in one line. The traditions gave very different answers about what work is. But across the texts we read, the same rhythm kept showing up: do the work with care, then stop. The Benedictine hours, the Sabbath, Friday prayers, the observance days. Work well, then rest. Ecclesiastes says there's a season for everything, "and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Work had its season on this path. Tomorrow a new question begins.
